claims.claim: Gregory Thaumaturgus (c. 213–c. 270); bishop of Neocaesarea; Gothic invasions of Asia Minor in the 250s.
Canonical Letter answers discipline questions after the raids (captive food; captive women).
Gregory Thaumaturgus was a Christian bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus (modern northwest Turkey) in the 3rd century.
Gregory Thaumaturgus was born around AD 213 and died around AD 270.
Gregory Thaumaturgus was also known as Gregory of Neocaesarea and surnamed Thaumaturgus, meaning 'wonder-worker,' due to miracles he reputedly performed.
The work was written in response to the Gothic invasion of Pontus, which brought rape, pillage, and apostasy.
The epistle is addressed to an anonymous bishop, possibly of an Apostolic See such as Antioch, or possibly one of his suffragans.
The work resolves moral questions about Christians who ate with barbarian captors, women who were raped by invaders, and Christians who plundered their brethren during the invasion.
Gregory ruled that captives who ate with barbarians should not be treated as having eaten things offered to idols, since the barbarians were reported not to sacrifice to idols.
Women raped by barbarians were not to be treated as guilty of fornication unless they had previously led lewd lives.
Christians who plundered their brethren during the invasion were to be excommunicated.
The epistle contains eleven canons, though canon 11 is disputed as not authentic.
